messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Herrera is a 34-year-old prison guard who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle this job, this country, this life. She had come to the United States as a teenager after her family fled political violence in Central America. What still returns most sharply is one night at a roadside checkpoint when soldiers stopped the bus her family was riding. She remembers the smell before anything else: alcohol on a guard’s breath as he leaned into the aisle, shouting orders no one dared question. Men in uniform pulled passengers up by the arm, barked instructions, and searched bags while her mother kept whispering for her not to look up. Marisol can still hear the clipped commands and the metallic scrape of rifles against the bus frame. The memory is not fragmentary to her; it is painfully clear, and when it comes back she hears those voices as if they are in the room again. If she lets herself stay with it even briefly, she is flooded so fast she has to shut it down.

Over the years she built a life, married, and eventually took a job in a correctional facility, partly because the structure and steady pay mattered. She now recognizes that the setting itself keeps brushing against the old terror. At work, being given orders over the radio, passing supervisors in uniform, or catching alcohol on an inmate during intake can hit her with a jolt that feels wildly out of proportion to the moment. In those moments, the cue seems to tell her something immediate and damning about her life: that authority is still dangerous, that nowhere is truly safe, and that she has become someone who can never fully stand down. She does not experience these as reminders at first; she experiences them as danger. A sudden movement beside her on the unit can make her spin and tense before she has even registered what happened. In meetings she studies the room and takes the chair nearest the door or the wall, somewhere protected. Each time this happens, it confirms for her that the world really is dangerous, that people in positions of authority are never simply what they seem, and that her vigilance is the only sensible response.

Those beliefs have deepened over time. Marisol says she no longer feels like the person she was before; she used to think of herself as steady and capable, but now she feels organized around scanning, bracing, and managing herself. Because she is certain that safety depends on anticipating harm, she dwells for hours on how the checkpoint might have been prevented, replaying who should have sat where, what her family should have noticed sooner, what she herself should have done. She knows these thoughts go nowhere, yet she returns to them as if one more pass might finally produce protection. The same distrust shapes her days at work: she avoids lingering near higher-ranking officers when she can, keeps interactions brief with people in uniform outside her immediate duties, and tells herself this distance is necessary because people with power are dangerous beneath the surface.

Her efforts to control the distress have narrowed her world and, in doing so, seem to keep the past close. When the memory starts pressing in, she turns on loud music in the car after a shift or leaves the television blaring at home so she does not have to hear her own mind. She cuts off images and sounds before they build, but the effect is temporary; the checkpoint returns with the same vividness, the same shouted orders in her head, the same wave of feeling that makes her stop mid-thought. After difficult shifts, especially if a supervisor has corrected her sharply or an inmate has reeked of liquor, she goes home and drowns the evening in noise, then later lies awake with the memory even more charged. She has begun to notice that the more she tries not to think, not to feel, not to be near reminders, the more quickly she reacts the next day to movement, uniforms, and commands.

Her hyperalertness also feeds the memory in a way she finds humiliating. On the prison floor she is constantly keyed up, tracking bodies and tone of voice, and in that keyed-up state the old scene comes back more easily and with more force. Living at that pitch of alarm, she finds the unit crowded with warning signals she cannot filter out; the smell of liquor, a clipped command, or a uniform in her peripheral vision all stand out at once, as if her sense of danger is teaching her what to notice. Once the memory is there, it strengthens her conviction that people cannot be trusted and that she has lost something essential of herself. Then those convictions make the next command from a superior officer sound less like routine supervision and more like the start of something coercive. By now even entering briefing rooms with rows of uniforms can feel loaded before anyone has spoken. She notices alcohol smell from astonishing distances. She interprets this sensitivity as proof that threat is everywhere, not as a symptom.

The strain has reached her marriage. Her husband has complained that she comes home and immediately turns on the television to full volume, barely speaking, and chooses restaurants by where she can sit with her back protected. She recently startled so hard when a coworker stepped beside her unexpectedly that she shoved a clipboard to the ground and burst into tears afterward in the restroom, ashamed and shaken by how overwhelmed she felt. What brought her in was not one dramatic crisis but the sense that her life is shrinking around these reactions. She is frightened that if this continues she will either lose her job or disappear into someone she does not recognize. What she hopes, cautiously, is not to erase what happened, but to stop living as if the checkpoint is still waiting around every corner.
